lesson.intro: Wi-Fi swaps the cable for radio: signals fade through walls, neighbors share the air, and anyone in range can listen. This pack covers RF basics, channels in 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz, SSIDs and service sets, the 802.11 standards and an overview of wireless encryption.
objectives: Describe frequency, wavelength, amplitude, antenna gain and EIRP
Interpret dBm, calculate SNR and identify interference
Plan nonoverlapping channels and tell SSID, BSSID, BSS, ESS and IBSS apart
Trace how a client discovers, authenticates, associates and gets keys
Compare WEP, WPA, WPA2 and WPA3, Personal and Enterprise

sections.title: RF basics: frequency, wavelength and amplitude
sections.key: Higher frequency means a shorter wavelength and shorter range: 2.4 GHz reaches farthest and passes walls best, while 5 and 6 GHz cells are smaller but far less crowded.
sections.body:
A coffee shop's Wi-Fi is fine near the counter and useless by the back wall. Wi-Fi sends data as **radio frequency (RF)** waves: an antenna radiates an electromagnetic wave outward, like ripples from a pebble, and the receiver's antenna turns it back into a signal.

[[visual]]

Wi-Fi uses three unlicensed **bands**:

[[visual 2]]

Lower frequencies travel farther and pass walls more easily. Higher ones fade faster, so 5 and 6 GHz cells are smaller, but those bands offer more channels, less interference and higher speeds.

Obstacles act predictably: **absorption** (drywall, concrete, water, people soak up energy), **reflection** (metal such as elevators, filing cabinets and mirrors bounces it) and scattering on rough surfaces. That back wall may be absorbing most of the signal.

visual.title: Three properties of a wave
rows: Cycles per second, in **hertz** (Hz); Wi-Fi uses gigahertz, billions per second
The physical length of one cycle; higher frequency means shorter wavelength
The height of the wave: its strength, which shrinks with distance and obstacles

sections.pitfall: Treating 5 GHz as faster Wi-Fi with better range. It is faster and far less crowded, but each cell is smaller, so a 5 GHz design needs APs closer together.

check.question: An AP broadcasts on both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz at the same power. Which statement is usually true?
choices: The 5 GHz signal reaches farther and penetrates walls better
Both bands have exactly the same range
The 2.4 GHz signal reaches farther and penetrates walls better
Neither band is affected by walls
check.explanation: Lower frequencies lose less energy over distance and through obstacles, so 2.4 GHz covers a larger area. 5 GHz trades some range for many more channels and less interference.

sections.title: Antennas, power and coverage
sections.key: An antenna focuses energy rather than adding it; EIRP = transmit power minus cable loss plus antenna gain, and each doubling of distance costs about 6 dB.
sections.body:
Two identical APs give very different coverage: one on an open-office ceiling, one on the wall at the end of a long warehouse aisle. The difference is the **antenna**.

An antenna creates no energy; it shapes where energy goes. **Antenna gain**, in **dBi**, compares it with an ideal antenna radiating equally everywhere. More gain means a tighter beam: stronger one way, weaker elsewhere.

[[visual]]

What leaves the antenna is the **EIRP** (effective isotropic radiated power). Regulators cap it, so you cannot just bolt on a bigger antenna.

[[visual 2]]

In open air the signal spreads over a growing sphere, so strength falls with the square of distance:

[[visual 3]]

Coverage is two-way: a loud AP can reach a phone that cannot shout back, one reason to keep AP power moderate.

visual.title: Antenna types
rows: All around horizontally, like a doughnut
A ceiling AP covering the room around it
Wall-mounted, covering the area in front
A long hallway or a link to a nearby building

visual.title: EIRP

steps.label: Start with the radio's transmit power

visual.result: EIRP = Tx power - cable loss + antenna gain = 20 dBm

visual.title: Received power as distance doubles (open air)
visual.caption: Measured against the power at 10 m. Walls and bodies add their own losses on top.

sections.pitfall: Thinking a high-gain antenna adds power. Gain only focuses the same energy into a narrower area, so coverage gets longer in one direction and weaker everywhere else.

check.question: A radio transmits at 20 dBm through a cable with 3 dB of loss into an antenna with 6 dBi gain. What is the EIRP?
check.explanation: EIRP = transmit power - cable loss + antenna gain = 20 - 3 + 6 = 23 dBm. Forgetting the cable loss gives 26 dBm.

sections.title: Signal strength, noise and interference
sections.key: Signal strength is in dBm, where closer to zero is stronger; SNR is signal minus noise, and same-channel or overlapping-channel APs cut into it.
sections.body:
Received signals are tiny, so they are measured in **dBm** (decibels relative to 1 mW). Every **+3 dB doubles** the power, **-3 dB halves** it, and 10 dB is a factor of ten. Received Wi-Fi signals are negative, and **closer to zero is stronger**: -55 dBm beats -75 dBm. Client tools often call this **RSSI**.

[[visual]]

What matters is how far the signal stands above the **noise floor**: the **signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)**. More SNR allows faster data rates; aim for about 25 dB or more for voice.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

Non-Wi-Fi sources also interfere: microwave ovens, Bluetooth, cordless phones and baby monitors in 2.4 GHz, weather radar in parts of 5 GHz.

A radio cannot detect collisions while transmitting, so 802.11 is **half duplex** and uses **CSMA/CA**:

[[visual 4]]

visual.title: Received signal strength
rows: The usual minimum target for voice and video
At or near the noise floor, the background RF energy

items.title: Co-channel interference
points: They take turns and share airtime

visual.title: CSMA/CA

steps.label: Listen until the channel is clear

visual.caption: More devices on one channel means more waiting.

sections.pitfall: Reading dBm like ordinary numbers. -80 dBm is much weaker than -60 dBm (100 times less power), because the scale is logarithmic and negative.

check.question: A laptop reports a signal of -62 dBm and a noise floor of -90 dBm. What is the SNR?
check.explanation: SNR is the signal minus the noise in dB: -62 - (-90) = 28 dB. That is a healthy margin, enough for most applications including voice.

sections.title: Channels and the 1, 6, 11 rule
sections.key: In 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap; 5 GHz 20 MHz channels never overlap, and 6 GHz adds 59 more.
sections.body:
A band is divided into numbered **channels**. In 2.4 GHz, channel centers are only 5 MHz apart, but each signal is 20 to 22 MHz wide, so channel 3 spills across channels 1 to 5.

[[visual]]

In the US (channels 1 to 11), only **1, 6 and 11** do not overlap. Use only those, and never bond 2.4 GHz channels to 40 MHz: there is no room.

[[visual 2]]

Middle 5 GHz channels need **DFS** (dynamic frequency selection): the AP listens for radar and must leave the channel if it hears any, so its clients briefly disconnect.

**Channel width** is a trade-off. Bonding into 40 or 80 MHz doubles or quadruples one client's peak speed but leaves fewer nonoverlapping channels for neighbors. In dense offices, 20 or 40 MHz often wins overall.

visual.title: 2.4 GHz: each signal spans about 22 MHz
visual.caption: Centers sit 5 MHz apart, so every channel overlaps its four nearest neighbors.

visual.title: The three bands
rows: North America uses 1 to 11; much of the world 1 to 13
1200 MHz added in the US; Wi-Fi 6E and 7 devices only

sections.pitfall: Picking less busy 2.4 GHz channels such as 3 or 9. They overlap their neighbors and cause adjacent-channel interference, which hurts more than sharing 1, 6 or 11.

check.question: Which set of 2.4 GHz channels can three neighboring APs use without overlapping in the US?
check.explanation: Channels are 5 MHz apart but signals are about 20 to 22 MHz wide, so channels must be five numbers apart to avoid overlap. With channels 1 to 11 available, 1, 6 and 11 is the only clean set of three.

sections.title: SSID, BSSID and service sets
sections.key: SSID is the network name, BSSID the AP radio's MAC; a BSS is one AP and its clients, an ESS many APs sharing an SSID, an IBSS no AP.
sections.body:
A phone's Wi-Fi menu lists names like "Office" and "Guest". Each is an **SSID** (service set identifier), up to 32 characters and not unique: every AP in the building can advertise "Office".

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

When a client **roams** within an ESS, the SSID stays the same while the BSSID (and usually the channel) changes.

One AP can offer several SSIDs, such as "Staff" in VLAN 10 and "Guest" in VLAN 30. It acts like several logical APs, **one BSSID per SSID**, and its switch port must be an **802.1Q trunk** carrying those VLANs. They still share one radio and channel, so more SSIDs add no capacity.

visual.title: 802.11 service set terms
rows: A unique identifier based on the AP radio's MAC address, carried in frames
One AP and the clients **associated** with it, on one channel
One AP's coverage area, or cell
The wired network behind the APs; the AP maps each SSID to a VLAN
Several APs with the same SSID, each its own BSS and channel, linked by the DS
Ad hoc: clients talk directly with no AP; does not scale

visual.title: One ESS, two BSSs
visual.caption: Both APs advertise SSID "Office" with different BSSIDs, such as d4:20:6d:90:ad:20 and e6:22:47:af:c3:70.

sections.deeper: APs can also run special modes. A **repeater** extends a cell without a cable by relaying traffic to a wired AP. A **workgroup bridge** acts as a wireless client on behalf of wired-only devices plugged into it. **Outdoor bridges** link buildings point to point or point to multipoint, often with directional antennas. In a **mesh**, APs relay traffic wirelessly hop by hop back to one wired AP.
sections.pitfall: Treating a hidden SSID as security. The name still travels in client probes and association frames, so any capture tool reveals it. Real protection comes from WPA2 or WPA3.

check.question: A phone roams from AP1 to AP2 inside one ESS. What changes?
choices: The VLAN the phone belongs to
check.explanation: In an ESS every AP advertises the same SSID, but each BSS has its own BSSID based on that AP's radio MAC. Roaming moves the client to a new BSS, so the BSSID changes; the SSID and VLAN stay the same.

sections.title: How a client finds and joins a WLAN
sections.key: A client finds an AP through beacons or probes, then authenticates, associates and runs the four-way handshake; only then can it send DHCP and other data.
sections.body:
You open a laptop in a new office and "Office" appears a moment later. A short exchange of 802.11 frames made that happen.

[[visual]]

Each AP sends a **beacon** per SSID about ten times a second: **passive scanning** is listening for them. Sending a **probe request** and getting a **probe response** is **active scanning**.

[[visual 2]]

The **four-way handshake** proves both sides know the key and builds fresh session keys; the passphrase never crosses the air. When a client moves and another AP in the ESS sounds better, it **roams** with a reassociation request.

A **hidden SSID** is beaconed with a blank name, so clients must send probe requests naming it, and any listener learns it.

visual.title: 802.11 frame types
rows: Running the WLAN: beacons, probes, authentication, association
Helping delivery: ACKs, RTS/CTS to reserve the channel

messages.label: Authentication
messages.detail: open system, or SAE with WPA3

messages.note: Four-way handshake builds the encryption keys

messages.label: DHCP Discover
messages.detail: a data frame, bridged to the SSID's VLAN

sections.pitfall: Thinking associated means connected. With WPA2 or WPA3 the four-way handshake must still finish, and DHCP must still give an address, before any IP traffic works.

check.question: Which 802.11 frame does an AP send about ten times per second to advertise each SSID it offers?
check.explanation: Beacons are management frames that APs send periodically for every SSID, carrying the SSID, BSSID, rates and security settings. Clients send probe requests; ACKs are control frames.

sections.title: 802.11 standards: a, b, g, n, ac, ax and be
sections.key: Client and AP need a shared standard and band: 802.11b and g use 2.4 GHz, a and ac only 5 GHz, n and ax both; ax adds 6 GHz.
sections.body:
An old scanner that supports only 802.11b/g can never join a 5 GHz-only SSID. That is why the exam wants the band of each amendment.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Data sheets list amendments with slashes: "802.11a/b/g/n/ac" supports all five. Maximum rates are theoretical; real throughput is usually under half, because the air is shared and half duplex.

Rates change on the fly: as SNR falls, both sides step down to slower, more robust rates. Beacons go out at the lowest **mandatory (basic)** rate, so disabling very low legacy rates frees airtime.

visual.title: Milestones
rows: **MIMO** (several antennas, several spatial streams) and 40 MHz channels
80 and 160 MHz channels, downlink **MU-MIMO** (several clients at once)
**OFDMA**: splits a channel into small resource units so many clients send at once; uplink MU-MIMO; built for crowded places
320 MHz channels in 6 GHz and multi-link operation across bands

sections.tip: Memory hook: b and g are the old 2.4 GHz pair, a and ac are 5 GHz only, n and ax do both (ax adds 6 GHz as 6E).
sections.pitfall: Assuming a new AP makes old clients faster. An 802.11g scanner still talks 802.11g at 2.4 GHz to an 802.11ax AP, and slow legacy clients use up extra airtime.

check.question: Which amendment operates only in the 5 GHz band?
check.explanation: 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) is 5 GHz only. 802.11b and 802.11g are 2.4 GHz only, and 802.11n uses both bands. 802.11a is the other 5 GHz-only amendment.

sections.title: Wireless security goals: from WEP to WPA
sections.key: Wi-Fi has no physical boundary, so it needs authentication, encryption and integrity; WEP (RC4) is broken and WPA's TKIP was only a stopgap.
sections.body:
To sniff a wired network you need a cable in a port. Wi-Fi frames reach anyone in range, including the parking lot. So a WLAN needs three things:

[[visual]]

The standards evolved because the early ones failed:

[[visual 2]]

WPA, WPA2 and WPA3 are **Wi-Fi Alliance certifications**, not IEEE amendments: devices certified for the same version are tested to work together.

Open guest networks are still common. Anyone nearby can read their traffic unless the AP supports **Enhanced Open (OWE)**, which encrypts each client's traffic without a password, or users rely on HTTPS and VPNs.

visual.title: Three security goals
rows: Only allowed users and devices join, and clients can trust the AP is real
A **message integrity check (MIC)**, computed with the key, makes tampered frames fail and get dropped

visual.title: The early standards
rows: RC4 with static keys shared by everyone
Broken: cracked in minutes. Never use it
**TKIP**: per-frame keys, a MIC and a sequence counter on WEP hardware, a software upgrade
Interim Wi-Fi Alliance fix while 802.11i was written; deprecated

sections.pitfall: Relying on MAC filtering or a hidden SSID for security. MAC addresses are visible in every frame and easy to spoof. Only WPA2 or WPA3 encryption actually protects the traffic.

check.question: Which wireless security option should never be used because its encryption is easily broken?
check.explanation: WEP's RC4-based design with static keys can be cracked in minutes. WPA2 with AES and WPA3 are the modern choices, and Enterprise mode adds per-user authentication through 802.1X.

sections.title: WPA2 and WPA3: CCMP, GCMP, SAE and Enterprise mode
sections.key: WPA2 uses AES-CCMP; WPA3 adds SAE in place of the shared-key handshake, mandatory protected management frames, and GCMP. Enterprise mode gives every user their own login.
sections.body:
**WPA2** is the full 802.11i standard, built on **AES-CCMP**: AES in counter mode for encryption plus CBC-MAC as the MIC.

**WPA3** (2018) adds protections:

- **SAE** (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) replaces the WPA2 pre-shared key exchange. A captured WPA2-Personal handshake allows millions of offline password guesses; with SAE each guess needs a live exchange, and past sessions stay safe if the password leaks (**forward secrecy**).
- **Protected Management Frames (PMF)** are required, so attackers cannot forge deauthentication frames.
- **GCMP** (AES Galois/Counter Mode, GMAC as the MIC) is the cipher the Cisco books pair with WPA3.
- 6 GHz allows only WPA3 or Enhanced Open.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

items.title: Personal
points: One shared passphrase: PSK, or SAE in WPA3
A departing employee still knows it

items.title: Enterprise
points: Each user logs in with their own credentials (an EAP method)
Remove one user without touching anyone else

visual.title: WPA, WPA2, WPA3
rows: Yes (per the Cisco books; GCMP-256 in 192-bit mode)
visual.caption: Staff: WPA3- or WPA2-Enterprise. Small sites: WPA3- or WPA2-Personal with a long passphrase. Never WEP or WPA.

sections.pitfall: Assuming WPA3-Personal gives each user their own password. It still uses one shared passphrase; SAE only protects it better. Per-user logins need Enterprise mode with 802.1X.

check.question: Which encryption and integrity method is the basis of WPA2?
check.explanation: WPA2 implements IEEE 802.11i with AES-CCMP: AES counter mode encryption plus a CBC-MAC integrity check. RC4 with static keys is WEP, and TKIP was the WPA stopgap.

sections.title: Putting it together: a small office WLAN
sections.key: A good small-office WLAN uses 1, 6 and 11 in 2.4 GHz, separate 5 GHz channels, moderate power, slightly overlapping cells and few SSIDs, all as one ESS.
sections.body:
A small office needs Wi-Fi on one floor: about 40 staff, video calls all day, a meeting room and a lobby.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

In larger networks a WLC or cloud controller automates channel and power choices (Cisco Radio Resource Management), but the reasoning is the same. When users complain of slow Wi-Fi despite full bars, think airtime, not signal: too many APs on one channel, too many SSIDs, or legacy 802.11b/g clients forcing slow rates.

visual.title: Three APs, one ESS
visual.caption: 2.4 GHz channel / 5 GHz channel on each AP. The same SSIDs everywhere let clients roam.

visual.title: Design choices
rows: Cells overlap a little (often 15 to 20% at -67 dBm)
Clients roam to the next AP before the old signal becomes unusable
No neighbors share or overlap a channel; with more APs, reuse far apart or turn some radios off
5 GHz on different 20 or 40 MHz channels
Where modern clients belong; **band steering** nudges them there
Huge cells make more APs share each channel, and clients cling to distant APs
Each SSID beacons about ten times a second at a low rate, burning airtime on every channel
One ESS, so clients roam smoothly

sections.tip: Full bars but slow is usually an airtime problem (a shared channel, many SSIDs, slow legacy clients), not a signal problem.
sections.pitfall: Turning every AP up to maximum power to fix coverage. Bigger cells mean more APs share each channel and clients cling to distant APs; add or move APs instead.

activity.title: Build the Staff SSID
activity.prompt: On the controller, create the "Staff" WLAN, bind it to the existing staff interface (VLAN 20), set WPA2 with AES and a passphrase (PSK), choose Gold QoS, then enable it, apply, and test that the laptop joins. As you go, say which design decision from this section each setting puts into practice.

check.question: Three APs in a small office all use channel 6 at maximum power. Users see strong signal but slow Wi-Fi. What is the best first fix?
choices: Move the APs to channels 1, 6 and 11 and reduce transmit power
Add a fourth AP on channel 6
Bond the 2.4 GHz channels to 40 MHz
check.explanation: All three APs share one channel, so they contend for the same airtime (co-channel interference). Separate channels and smaller cells fix it. Another AP on channel 6 adds contention, and 40 MHz in 2.4 GHz makes overlap worse.

keyTerms.definition: Cycles per second of a wave, in hertz; Wi-Fi uses the 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz bands.
The height of a wave, which represents signal strength.
Power relative to 1 mW on a log scale; +3 dB doubles power, and received Wi-Fi signals are negative values.
Signal-to-noise ratio: received signal minus the noise floor, in dB. Higher allows faster data rates.
Channels whose frequency ranges do not overlap: 1, 6 and 11 in 2.4 GHz (US); all 20 MHz channels in 5 GHz.
The human-readable wireless network name, up to 32 characters and not unique.
Unique identifier of a BSS, based on the AP radio MAC address.
One AP and its associated clients on one channel.
Multiple BSSs sharing an SSID and connected by a distribution system, so clients can roam.
Ad hoc wireless network where clients talk directly with no AP.
Wi-Fi's half-duplex access method: listen, back off randomly, transmit, and expect an ACK.
Current Wi-Fi security standard; Personal mode uses SAE instead of a pre-shared key handshake.
Effective isotropic radiated power: transmit power minus cable loss plus antenna gain, in dBm.
Antenna gain compared with an ideal antenna that radiates equally in all directions.
Management frame an AP sends about ten times a second per SSID, advertising the SSID, BSSID, rates and security.
The exchange that makes a client a member of an AP's BSS, after discovery and 802.11 authentication.
AES counter mode encryption with a CBC-MAC integrity check; the basis of WPA2.
AES Galois/Counter Mode with a GMAC integrity check; stronger and more efficient, associated with WPA3.

summary: Higher frequency means shorter range: 2.4 GHz reaches farthest; 5 and 6 GHz have more channels and less interference.
dBm closer to zero is stronger; SNR is signal minus noise; EIRP = power - cable loss + antenna gain.
Use 2.4 GHz channels 1, 6 and 11 only; 5 GHz 20 MHz channels never overlap; 6 GHz adds 59.
SSID is the name, BSSID the AP radio MAC; BSS one AP, ESS many APs with one SSID, IBSS ad hoc.
Clients discover, authenticate, associate, then run the four-way handshake before DHCP.
b/g are 2.4 GHz, a/ac 5 GHz, n and ax both (ax adds 6 GHz). WEP and WPA are out; WPA2 is AES-CCMP; WPA3 adds SAE, PMF and GCMP.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why their Wi-Fi can show full bars and still be slow, using channels, airtime and interference in your answer.

questions.question: An AP sends on 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz at the same power. Which statement is true?
choices: 5 GHz reaches farther because its wavelength is shorter
5 GHz penetrates concrete better than 2.4 GHz
2.4 GHz reaches farther and passes through walls better
Both bands lose strength at exactly the same rate
questions.explanation: Lower frequency signals lose less energy over distance and through obstacles, so 2.4 GHz covers more area. 5 GHz has a shorter wavelength, which is exactly why it fades faster.

questions.question: Which property of a radio wave represents its strength?
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the height of the wave, which corresponds to signal strength. Frequency is cycles per second and wavelength is the length of one cycle.

questions.question: Roughly how long is one wavelength of a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi signal?
questions.explanation: Wavelength is the speed of light divided by frequency: 300,000,000 m/s / 2,400,000,000 Hz = 0.125 m, or 12.5 cm. About 6 cm is the wavelength of 5 GHz.

questions.question: Which band did Wi-Fi 6E add for Wi-Fi?
questions.explanation: Wi-Fi 6E is 802.11ax extended into the 6 GHz band (5.925 to 7.125 GHz in the US). Wi-Fi 7 also uses it.

questions.question: Which received signal strength is the strongest?
questions.explanation: Received signals are negative dBm values, and closer to zero is stronger. -55 dBm is far stronger than -67 dBm, while -90 dBm is near the noise floor.

questions.question: A client measures a signal of -70 dBm and a noise floor of -95 dBm. What is the SNR in dB?
questions.explanation: SNR is signal minus noise: -70 - (-95) = 25 dB. That is roughly the minimum usually recommended for voice over Wi-Fi.

questions.question: An AP's transmit power is raised from 14 dBm to 17 dBm. What happens to the power in milliwatts?
questions.explanation: Each +3 dB is about a doubling of power (14 dBm is about 25 mW, 17 dBm about 50 mW). A +10 dB change would be tenfold.

questions.question: Two neighboring APs use 2.4 GHz channels 1 and 3. Which problem does this create?
choices: Co-channel interference, where the APs politely share airtime
Adjacent-channel interference, where overlapping signals corrupt each other
No problem, because the channel numbers differ
A duplex mismatch between the APs
questions.explanation: Channels 1 and 3 overlap, so each AP's signal looks like noise to the other and frames get corrupted. Same-channel APs at least hear each other and take turns, which is less damaging.

questions.question: Users near the break room lose Wi-Fi every time someone heats lunch. Which band and source is the likely culprit?
choices: 5 GHz, interference from a cordless phone base
2.4 GHz, interference from a microwave oven
questions.explanation: Microwave ovens operate around 2.45 GHz and leak enough energy to swamp nearby 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. Moving those clients to 5 GHz is the usual fix.

questions.question: Why does 802.11 use collision avoidance (CSMA/CA) with acknowledgments instead of collision detection like half-duplex Ethernet?
choices: Wi-Fi runs full duplex, so collisions cannot happen
Collision detection would require a WLC
A radio cannot reliably detect a collision while it is transmitting on the same frequency
questions.explanation: A transmitting radio drowns out its own receiver on that channel, so it cannot sense a collision as it happens. Wi-Fi therefore backs off randomly before sending and relies on an ACK for each unicast frame; a missing ACK triggers a retransmission.

questions.question: How many nonoverlapping channels are available in the 2.4 GHz band in the US?
questions.explanation: Only channels 1, 6 and 11 avoid overlapping each other. Every other channel spills into one of them.

questions.question: All four APs in the exhibit can hear each other. Which AP's channel causes adjacent-channel interference?
questions.code:
AP name     Band      Channel   Width
AP-Lobby    2.4 GHz   1         20 MHz
AP-East     2.4 GHz   6         20 MHz
AP-West     2.4 GHz   9         20 MHz
AP-Conf     2.4 GHz   11        20 MHz
questions.explanation: Channel 9 overlaps both channel 6 and channel 11, so AP-West interferes with AP-East and AP-Conf. Channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap. The fourth AP should reuse one of those three channels, as far away as possible from its twin.

questions.question: Which two statements about the 5 GHz band are true? (Choose two.)
choices: Its 20 MHz channels do not overlap each other
It has only three nonoverlapping channels
Some of its channels require DFS to avoid radar
Bonding to 80 MHz increases the number of nonoverlapping channels
questions.explanation: 5 GHz channels are spaced so that 20 MHz channels never overlap, and channels 52 to 144 require dynamic frequency selection. 5 GHz has shorter range than 2.4 GHz, and wider channels reduce the number of separate channels.

questions.question: An engineer configures all 2.4 GHz radios for 40 MHz channel width to get more speed. What is the result in a building with several APs?
choices: Almost no room for nonoverlapping channels, so neighboring APs overlap and interfere
Automatic move to the 5 GHz band
questions.explanation: The 2.4 GHz band is only about 83 MHz wide. A 40 MHz channel consumes most of it, so neighboring APs cannot avoid overlapping. Keep 2.4 GHz at 20 MHz and use wider channels only in 5 or 6 GHz.

questions.question: Why might a dense office choose 20 or 40 MHz channels in 5 GHz instead of 80 MHz?
choices: Narrower channels leave more nonoverlapping channels, so neighboring APs interfere less
Wider channels do not work in 5 GHz
Narrower channels give every client a higher peak speed
80 MHz channels are only allowed outdoors
questions.explanation: Wider channels raise the peak rate for one client but reduce the number of separate channels. With many APs close together, more channels mean less co-channel interference and better total performance.

questions.question: What is an SSID?
choices: The MAC address of the AP radio
The human-readable name of a wireless network
The encryption key for the WLAN
questions.explanation: The SSID is the network name users see, up to 32 characters. The AP radio's MAC-based identifier is the BSSID.

questions.question: What is the BSSID of a basic service set?
choices: A unique identifier based on the AP radio's MAC address
The SSID with the VLAN number appended
The IP address of the WLC
The channel number used by the BSS
questions.explanation: Each BSS is identified by a BSSID derived from the AP radio MAC address. Multiple SSIDs on one radio each get their own BSSID, usually by incrementing the last digit of the MAC.

questions.question: Match each 802.11 term to its description.

pairs.right: One AP and its associated clients on one channel
Several APs sharing an SSID, linked by the wired network
Clients talking directly to each other with no AP
The wired network the APs connect to
The coverage area, or cell, of one AP

questions.explanation: A BSS centers on one AP, an ESS joins several BSSs through the distribution system so clients can roam, and an IBSS (ad hoc) has no AP at all.

questions.question: One AP must offer SSID "Staff" in VLAN 10 and SSID "Guest" in VLAN 30. How should the switch port connected to the AP be configured, and what does the AP advertise?
choices: An access port in VLAN 10; one BSSID for both SSIDs
An access port in VLAN 30; two different channels
A routed port; one SSID per channel
An 802.1Q trunk carrying VLANs 10 and 30; a separate BSSID for each SSID
questions.explanation: Each SSID maps to a VLAN, so the AP needs a trunk carrying both VLANs. The AP acts as two logical APs on the same radio and channel, each with its own BSSID.

questions.question: Two laptops at a conference exchange files over Wi-Fi with no access point involved. Which topology is this?
questions.explanation: An independent basic service set (ad hoc network) lets clients talk directly with no AP. BSS and ESS both require at least one AP.

questions.question: Match each 802.11 amendment to the bands it uses.
questions.explanation: b and g are the 2.4 GHz pair, a and ac are 5 GHz only, and n and ax work in both bands, with ax extending into 6 GHz as Wi-Fi 6E.

questions.question: Put these 802.11 amendments in the order they were introduced, oldest first.
A barcode scanner supports only 802.11b/g. The new SSID is offered only on the APs' 5 GHz radios. What happens?
choices: The scanner cannot connect, because b and g work only in 2.4 GHz
The AP converts the scanner to 802.11a
questions.explanation: 802.11b and 802.11g exist only in 2.4 GHz. A client and AP must share both an amendment and a band, so the scanner needs the SSID on a 2.4 GHz radio.

questions.question: Which two 802.11 amendments operate only in the 5 GHz band? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: 802.11a and 802.11ac are 5 GHz only. 802.11b and g are 2.4 GHz only, and 802.11n works in both bands.

questions.question: Put these Wi-Fi security standards in order from oldest (weakest) to newest.
questions.explanation: WEP was broken, WPA with TKIP was an interim fix, WPA2 brought AES-CCMP, and WPA3 added SAE and mandatory protected management frames.

questions.question: Which encryption does WPA2 use?
questions.explanation: WPA2 implements 802.11i with AES-CCMP. RC4 with static keys is WEP, and TKIP was WPA's interim method.

questions.question: What does WPA3-Personal use in place of the WPA2 pre-shared key handshake?
questions.explanation: SAE resists offline dictionary attacks against the passphrase and provides forward secrecy. 802.1X with RADIUS is Enterprise mode, not Personal.

questions.question: A company wants every employee to sign in to Wi-Fi with their own credentials, and to cut off one person's access without changing anything for everyone else. What should it deploy?
choices: An open SSID with MAC filtering
WPA2 or WPA3-Enterprise using 802.1X and a RADIUS server
questions.explanation: Enterprise mode authenticates each user through 802.1X against a RADIUS server, so access can be revoked per person. Personal modes, even WPA3 with SAE, still use one shared passphrase.

questions.question: A manager suggests hiding the SSID instead of setting up WPA3. Why is that not real security?
choices: Hidden SSIDs cannot be joined by anyone
Hiding the SSID forces the network to use WEP
Hidden SSIDs only work in 2.4 GHz
The SSID still appears in client probe and association frames, and hiding it encrypts nothing
questions.explanation: Any wireless capture reveals a hidden SSID as soon as a client connects, and hiding the name does nothing to encrypt traffic. WPA2 or WPA3 is what protects the data.

questions.question: An office has three APs, all on 2.4 GHz channel 11 at maximum power. Signal is strong everywhere but throughput is poor at busy times. What is the best first change?
choices: Add a fourth AP on channel 11
Spread the APs across channels 1, 6 and 11 and lower the transmit power
Switch the 2.4 GHz radios to 40 MHz
Add a separate SSID for each AP
questions.explanation: All three APs share one channel, so they and their clients contend for the same airtime. Separate channels and smaller cells reduce co-channel interference. Wider 2.4 GHz channels and more SSIDs both make things worse.

questions.question: Why does advertising many SSIDs on every AP hurt performance?
choices: Each SSID needs its own channel
Clients can only see one SSID at a time
Each SSID sends its own beacons at a low data rate, using up airtime on every channel
Each SSID halves the AP's transmit power
questions.explanation: Every SSID is a separate BSS with its own beacons, sent about ten times per second at a low rate. Those beacons consume airtime that data could use, on every AP and channel.

questions.question: Why are neighboring AP cells designed to overlap a little instead of just touching?
choices: So that clients can roam to the next AP before the old signal becomes unusable
So that APs can share one channel
Because overlap increases the data rate
So that the SSIDs can be different
questions.explanation: A modest overlap at a good signal level (for example around -67 dBm) gives clients a strong next AP to roam to before the current one fades, which keeps calls up while moving.

questions.question: An AP radio transmits at 17 dBm. The cable to its external antenna loses 2 dB, and the antenna has 5 dBi of gain. What is the EIRP in dBm?
questions.explanation: EIRP = transmit power - cable loss + antenna gain = 17 - 2 + 5 = 20 dBm. Regulators limit EIRP, not just the radio's transmit power.

questions.question: Match each antenna to the job it suits best.

pairs.right: Ceiling AP covering the room around it
Wall-mounted, covering the area in front of it
A long hallway or a link to a nearby building

questions.explanation: Omnidirectional antennas cover all around, which suits ceiling APs. Directional antennas focus energy: a patch covers the area in front of a wall, a Yagi a long narrow area, and a dish the longest point-to-point links.

questions.question: A client moves from 10 meters to 20 meters away from an AP in open air. Roughly how much weaker is the signal it receives?
questions.explanation: Free-space loss follows the inverse square of distance: doubling the distance spreads the energy over four times the area, one quarter of the power, which is about 6 dB. Walls would add more loss on top.

questions.question: A laptop joins a WPA2-protected SSID using active scanning. Put the steps in order.
items: Client sends a probe request for the SSID
AP answers with a probe response
Four-way handshake builds the encryption keys
questions.explanation: The client discovers the AP (probe request and response), completes 802.11 authentication, associates, runs the four-way handshake to build encryption keys, and only then sends DHCP to get an IP address.

questions.question: An SSID is configured as hidden. How does a client that knows the name still join it, and what does that reveal?
choices: It reads the name from the beacons, so nothing is revealed
It sends probe requests that name the SSID, so anyone listening learns the name
It needs the AP's IP address instead of the SSID
It uses WEP to decrypt the hidden name
questions.explanation: Beacons for a hidden SSID leave the name blank, so the client sends probe requests that contain the SSID, and the AP answers. Those probes and the association frames carry the name in clear text, so any capture reveals it.

questions.question: Which 802.11 frame type includes beacons, probes and association requests?
questions.explanation: Beacons, probe requests and responses, authentication and association frames are management frames. Control frames include ACK, RTS and CTS; data frames carry user traffic.

questions.question: Which cipher suite does the Cisco CCNA material associate with WPA3, using AES with GMAC as its integrity check?
questions.explanation: GCMP is AES in Galois/Counter Mode with GMAC as the MIC, which the Cisco books list for WPA3. CCMP (AES with CBC-MAC) is WPA2's method, TKIP was WPA's stopgap, and RC4 belongs to WEP.

questions.question: Match each Wi-Fi security generation to its defining method.

pairs.right: RC4 with static keys, easily cracked
TKIP, an interim fix for old hardware
SAE and required protected management frames

questions.explanation: WEP used RC4 with static keys and is broken. WPA used TKIP to upgrade old hardware. WPA2 brought 802.11i AES-CCMP. WPA3 added SAE and mandatory protected management frames.

questions.question: Which two statements are true of WPA3-Personal compared with WPA2-Personal? (Choose two.)
choices: It uses SAE, which resists offline dictionary attacks on the passphrase
It gives every user an individual username and password
It uses TKIP for backward compatibility
questions.explanation: SAE makes every password guess require a live exchange, which defeats offline dictionary attacks, and WPA3 requires protected management frames. Personal mode still uses one shared passphrase and needs no RADIUS server, and TKIP is not allowed.

questions.question: An AP on 5 GHz channel 100 suddenly switches to channel 36, and its clients disconnect for a few seconds. What most likely happened?
choices: The AP detected radar and DFS rules forced it off the channel
A client requested a different channel
The AP ran out of BSSIDs
questions.explanation: Channels 52 to 144 require DFS. When the AP detects radar on its channel it must move off it, which briefly disrupts clients. Co-channel interference would slow things down but not force a channel change by law.

questions.question: Which 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) feature lets an AP serve several clients at the same moment by dividing a channel into small resource units?
questions.explanation: OFDMA splits a channel into resource units so several clients can send or receive short frames simultaneously, which is why Wi-Fi 6 helps in crowded places. MIMO uses multiple antennas, and DFS and CSMA/CA are unrelated.
